verdict.summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is a settings form with no review queue, so a developer can work end to end in minutes once signed in. The harder parts are choosing scopes (the default Composio list includes broad scopes such as repo and workflow), handling 8-hour access tokens, and planning around rate limits; a Marketplace listing adds real review-style requirements.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 45-90 min for a working connection with your own account; 1-2 days more if you add a Marketplace listing and publisher verification
verdict.time_to_first_connection: 15-30 min after you have a signed-in GitHub account
verdict.approval_wait: none for registering and using an OAuth app; Marketplace listing and publisher verification have no published timeline

gates.name: Your own account (development use)
gates.unlocks: You can register the app and connect your own GitHub account through it. Registration needs a signed-in GitHub account.
limits: Registration requires a signed-in GitHub account (no anonymous registration).
A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
Access tokens expire after 8 hours by default for new apps; refresh tokens last six months without use.

gates.name: Organization-owned app used by org members (no separate test-user allowlist found)
gates.unlocks: An app registered under an organization can be used by that organization's members. Outside collaborators depend on the org's policy for unapproved OAuth apps.
limits: Registration needs administrative access to the organization.
If the organization has an application policy, a member's request to use the app must be approved by an owner.
Rate limit is 5,000 requests per hour per app, shared with the authorizing user; 15,000 for apps owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization when the user is a member.
OAuth access-token requests are capped at 2,000 per hour across GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.
gates.time_to_reach: Under 1 hour once the org exists and you have admin access

gates.name: Public use (any GitHub user) and Marketplace listing
gates.unlocks: Any GitHub user can authorize the app. A public OAuth app needs no review. A Marketplace listing is a separate, optional step with review-style requirements.
limits: Public OAuth-app use needs no review; this is inferred from the pages read.
Marketplace listing needs a privacy policy link, a Marketplace Developer Agreement, and value beyond authentication.
Paid plans need a verified publisher organization (two-factor authentication and a verified domain).
Paid OAuth-app listings are expected to reach 200 users.
gates.time_to_reach: Public OAuth use: immediate after Gate 2. Marketplace listing: no published timeline.

steps.title: Sign in to GitHub and confirm the account
steps.detail: Sign in to the GitHub account that will own the app. Registration pages redirect anonymous visitors to sign-in, so you cannot register an app without an account.
gotchas: Use an account you will keep. The app is owned by this account unless you register it under an organization.

steps.title: Decide between an OAuth app and a GitHub App
steps.detail: GitHub's own comparison generally prefers GitHub Apps for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. Choose an OAuth app if you need to reach enterprise-level resources, since GitHub Apps cannot yet be granted permissions against an enterprise. This guide covers OAuth apps only.
gotchas: An OAuth app always acts as the authorizing user and cannot act on its own.
OAuth apps cannot request granular permissions, so reading issues or pull requests needs the broad repo scope.

steps.title: Open the OAuth app form under Developer settings
steps.detail: Click your profile photo, then Settings. In the left sidebar, click Developer settings, then OAuth apps, then New OAuth App. If this is your first app, the button reads Register a new application.
gotchas: The developer portal URL in the summary points to the GitHub App form (settings/apps/new). For an OAuth app, use the Developer settings path above.

steps.title: Fill in the registration form
steps.detail: Enter an Application name, the Homepage URL, and an optional Description. In Authorization callback URL, paste the exact callback URL from your Composio auth config. Up to 10 callback URIs can be registered if you need more than one.

values.label: Application name
values.value: Your app name (for example, your agent's name)

values.label: Authorization callback URL
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

values.label: Enable Device Flow
values.value: Leave unticked unless the app runs without a browser

gotchas: Callback URL must match exactly. GitHub documents exact matching for GitHub Apps; confirm it for OAuth apps by testing the flow (see open questions).
The expiring-user-token checkbox is ticked by default. Leave it ticked unless your auth SDK cannot refresh tokens.

steps.title: Register the app and copy the client credentials
steps.detail: Click Register application. Copy the Client ID from the app page and generate a client secret. Store the secret in your secrets manager; do not commit it to source control.

values.label: Client ID
values.value: From the app page after registration

values.label: Client secret
values.value: Generated on the app page; shown once

gotchas: If the app is registered under an organization, the org admin role is required to create it.

steps.title: Enter the client ID and secret in Composio
steps.detail: In Composio, create a custom auth config for the GitHub toolkit (slug: github) using your client ID and secret. Confirm the endpoints match the GitHub authorize and token URLs. Paste the Composio redirect URI into the GitHub app's callback URL if it differs from step 4.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Composio's managed config uses its own client and callback. Your own app needs its own callback registered, as above.

steps.title: Narrow the scope list before you connect
steps.detail: Compare the scopes your agent actually needs with Composio's default list (repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace). Drop any scope you do not use, because requested scopes are shown to every user on the consent form. Draft a one-line justification for each scope you keep.

values.label: Default Composio scopes
values.value: repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace

gotchas: repo gives read and write access to code, webhooks and collaborators across public and private repos.
Keep workflow only if the agent must create or update workflow files; GitHub refuses those writes without it.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start the connect flow in Composio using your own GitHub account. Check that the consent form lists the scopes you expect and that the callback returns to Composio. Confirm the access token is issued, and note its expiry.
gotchas: Tokens expire after 8 hours by default for new apps. Check that Composio refreshes them using the refresh token, which lasts six months without use.
The authorization code expires 10 minutes after it is issued. Complete the exchange promptly.
Use PKCE (S256) if your flow supports it; GitHub documents it for OAuth apps.

steps.title: Plan around OAuth rate limits
steps.detail: Estimate the requests per hour your agent will make per app and per user. The primary limit is 5,000 per hour per app, shared with the authorizing user's own requests. Organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud get 15,000 per hour for member requests.

values.label: Primary limit
values.value: 5,000 requests per hour per OAuth app

values.label: Enterprise Cloud org limit
values.value: 15,000 requests per hour (when the user is a member)

values.label: Token request limit
values.value: 2,000 OAuth access-token requests per hour across GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

gotchas: Limits are shared with the user's own GitHub use. Heavy interactive use of the same account can exhaust the budget.
Frequent token refreshes count toward the 2,000 per hour token-request limit.

steps.title: Set organization approval rules if the app is org-owned
steps.detail: If the app is registered under an organization, ask an organization owner to check the organization's policy on third-party OAuth apps. If the policy is active, each member's first authorization needs owner approval before it works.
gotchas: Outside collaborators can be blocked from requesting access to unapproved OAuth apps by the org's settings.
Owners set this in the organization's settings; the app registrant cannot change it.

steps.title: Decide whether you need a Marketplace listing
steps.detail: Public OAuth use does not need a review. Only a Marketplace listing needs the listing requirements: a Marketplace Developer Agreement, a privacy policy link, a description, a pricing plan, and value beyond authentication. Skip this step unless you want a Marketplace listing.
gotchas: Paid plans need a verified publisher organization with two-factor authentication and a verified domain.
GitHub expects a paid OAuth-app listing to reach 200 users.

steps.title: Prepare publisher verification (only for a paid or verified listing)
steps.detail: An organization owner submits a Request Verification form after enabling two-factor authentication for the organization and verifying its domain. GitHub reviews the request and notifies you when verification is complete. Only organization owners can create and submit Marketplace listings for org-owned apps.
gotchas: No review timeline is published. Plan for uncertainty in the calendar.
The GitHub App manager role does not grant the right to submit listings.

steps.title: Submit the Marketplace listing and wait for review
steps.detail: After you submit the Marketplace listing, GitHub reviews it against the listing requirements. Track the status in the Marketplace developer area. No review timeline was found in the sources.
gotchas: Free listings need only the general listing requirements; paid plans need the extra steps above.

requirements.detail: Required before any OAuth app can be registered.

requirements.item: Registration rights on the owning account or organization
requirements.detail: Personal account, or an organization where you have administrative access.

requirements.item: Callback URL that matches the Composio redirect URI
requirements.detail: Set in the Authorization callback URL field. Up to 10 callback URIs are allowed.
If the org has an application policy, owners must approve member requests to use unapproved OAuth apps.

requirements.item: Two-factor authentication and verified domain for publisher verification
requirements.detail: Required for a verified publisher, which paid Marketplace plans need.

requirements.item: Privacy policy link on Marketplace listing
requirements.detail: Listings must have a valid link to a privacy policy.

requirements.item: Value beyond authentication and webhooks for plan events
requirements.detail: Marketplace apps must integrate beyond authentication.

scopes.effect: Broadest scope: read and write access to code, webhooks, collaborators and deployments on public and private repos. Shown on consent. Fine-grained alternatives are not available to OAuth apps. Drop it unless the agent needs repo access.
Needed to create or update GitHub Actions workflow files; GitHub refuses those writes without it. Broad. Request only if needed.
Included in Composio's default list. The findings cover read:user (profile data); confirm the exact scope and what it allows.
Write access to gists. Keep only if the agent manages gists.
Access to notifications. Keep only if the agent reads them.
Access to projects. Keep only if the agent manages projects.
Access to codespaces. Keep only if the agent manages codespaces.

blockers.symptom: Member's authorization is blocked or waiting for an owner's approval
blockers.cause: The organization has an application policy for unapproved OAuth apps.
blockers.fix: Ask an organization owner to approve the app in the organization's OAuth app settings, or register the app under your personal account.

blockers.symptom: GitHub refuses to create or update workflow files through the app
blockers.cause: The workflow scope was not requested or granted.
blockers.fix: Add workflow to the scope list if the agent really needs it, then have users re-authorize.

blockers.symptom: Requests start failing with rate-limit errors
blockers.cause: The app and its user share a 5,000 requests per hour budget, and token requests are capped at 2,000 per hour.
blockers.fix: Cache results, reduce polling, and space out token refreshes. Organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud get a higher member limit of 15,000 per hour.

blockers.symptom: Connections stop working after about 8 hours
blockers.cause: New apps issue expiring access tokens by default, lasting 8 hours.
blockers.fix: Confirm that Composio refreshes tokens with the refresh token. If your SDK cannot refresh, untick the expiring-token option, though that changes token lifetime for future sign-ins only.

blockers.cause: The device flow allows 50 user-code submissions per hour per app.
blockers.fix: Only enable device flow for CLI-style apps, and throttle code requests.

composio.note: Start on Composio's managed GitHub OAuth config to get a working flow quickly. Move to your own OAuth app if you need your own client ID and callback URL, consent branding, narrower scopes than the default list (which includes repo and workflow), or a separate rate-limit budget. Your own app means the redirect URI shown in your Composio auth config must be registered on the GitHub app.

open_questions: The developer portal URL in the findings (github.com/settings/apps/new) is the GitHub App form, not the OAuth app form. This guide uses Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps instead; confirm the exact path in your account.

OAuth-app refresh-token steps were not fully read. The refresh request details come from the GitHub App page, so confirm the OAuth-app refresh request (client ID, client secret, refresh token, endpoint) in the official docs.

It is not confirmed whether OAuth-app callback matching is exact-match (documented for GitHub Apps only). Whether Composio's callback URL needs a specific path is also unconfirmed. Test the flow to confirm.
GitHub's OIDC discovery document was not confirmed; the probe timed out.

No review step for registering an OAuth app was found; this is inferred from the pages read, not confirmed by a source. No public-install cap or test-user allowlist for OAuth apps was found, so Gate 2 is based on organization membership and policy only.
Marketplace review and publisher verification have no published timelines.
The scope tiers (basic, sensitive, restricted) were not given in the findings; scope tiers are marked unknown. The live consent screen was not checked.
One Marketplace source URL in the findings (docs.docs.github.com) looks malformed. Its claim about 200 users for paid OAuth listings should be confirmed on the official docs.
Whether Composio handles token refresh for your own OAuth app was not checked.
